candidates.title: [Bug] EAGLE/NEXTN speculative decoding crashes scheduler on response_format (xgrammar type mismatch)
candidates.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When EAGLE/NEXTN speculative decoding is enabled and a request includes `response_format` (JSON schema / structured output), the scheduler crashes with a `TypeError` in `generate_token_bitmask`. This takes down the entire SGLang process, killing all in-flight requests on the node.

The crash is in `eagle_worker_v2.py:828` -> `spec_utils.py:675` -> `reasoner_grammar_backend.py:75` -> xgrammar's `fill_next_token_bitmask`, which receives an `ffi.Tensor` where it expects an `int`.

This is the same bug as #15050 which was auto-closed by the stale bot without a fix.

### Traceback

```
[2026-05-02 23:26:04 TP1] Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 3934, in run_scheduler_process
    scheduler.run_event_loop()
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 1505, in run_event_loop
    dispatch_event_loop(self)
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 3804, in dispatch_event_loop
    scheduler.event_loop_overlap()
  File "/opt/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/torch/utils/_contextlib.py", line 124, in decorate_context
    return func(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 1565, in event_loop_overlap
    ...
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py", line 828, in verify
    vocab_mask = generate_token_bitmask(
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/speculative/spec_utils.py", line 675, in generate_token_bitmask
    traverse_tree(
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/speculative/spec_utils.py", line 641, in traverse_tree
    dfs(0, retrieve_next_token, retrieve_next_sibling, -1)
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/speculative/spec_utils.py", line 618, in dfs
    grammar.fill_vocab_mask(allocate_token_bitmask, curr)
  File "/opt/sglang/python/sglang/srt/constrained/reasoner_grammar_backend.py", line 75, in fill_vocab_mask
    ...
  File "python/tvm_ffi/cython/function.pxi", line 929, in tvm_ffi.core.Function.__call__
TypeError: Mismatched type on argument #2 when calling: `xgrammar.tvm_ffi_binding.GrammarMatcher.fill_next_token_bitmask(0: xgrammar.tvm_ffi_binding.GrammarMatcher, 1: AnyView, 2: int, 3: bool) -> bool`. Expected `int` but got `ffi.Tensor`
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Launch SGLang with NEXTN speculative decoding enabled:
   ```
   speculative_algo: "NEXTN"
   speculative_num_steps: 2
   speculative_eagle_topk: 1
   speculative_num_draft_tokens: 3
   ```

2. Send a request with `response_format`:
   ```json
   {
     "model": "...",
     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "List 3 colors"}],
     "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "colors", "schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"colors": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}}}}}
   }
   ```

3. Scheduler crashes, SIGQUIT propagates to all TP workers, entire process dies.

### Impact

This is a production-critical bug. A single customer request with `response_format` crashes every node running EAGLE/NEXTN, causing cascading failures across a fleet. The crash is in the scheduler's hot path with no try/catch, so it takes down all concurrent requests.

### Environment

- SGLang: latest (morph-sglang-sm120:b12x-hicache image, based on upstream main)
- Model: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B NVFP4, TP=4
- Hardware: 4x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
- Speculative: NEXTN with eagle_topk=1, num_draft_tokens=3

### Suggested fix

The `generate_token_bitmask` in `spec_utils.py` calls `grammar.fill_vocab_mask(allocate_token_bitmask, curr)` where `curr` is the tree node index. In the EAGLE verify path, the bitmask allocation tensor is passed where xgrammar expects an integer index. The type conversion between the speculative tree's token indices and xgrammar's expected `int` argument is missing.

### Related issues

- #15050 (same bug, auto-closed by stale bot)
- #14462 (related data race in spec_v2 guided decoding)

candidates.title: [Benchmark] Qwen3.5-122B-A10B FP8 weights / bf16 KV on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120): 1,985 tok/s burst, MTP 2.75x, fp8 KV silent corruption finding
candidates.body:
Benchmarked **Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8** on 8x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120) via AWS g7e.48xlarge. This is a DeltaNet MoE model, and in my testing its SM120 bring-up was more complex than standard MoE (see [my M2.5 benchmarks in #18870](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/18870)). DeltaNet layers added attention backend, KV cache dtype, and caching constraints that did not appear in the M2.5 setup.

The short version: of the optimization paths I tested on this model + hardware combo, **MTP was the only one that materially improved performance**: 2.75x single-request speedup. FP8 KV produced corrupt output, CUDA graphs and HiCache were incompatible with this model's architecture, and DeepEP was blocked by g7e's PCIe topology.

I'm not contributing novel kernels here. I'm doing careful bring-up and reproducible characterization on SM120/g7e so others can avoid blind alleys. This is the fourth model in a series ([M2.5 in #18870](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/18870), GLM-5, Qwen3.5-397B, now 122B).

## Environment

| Component | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Instance | AWS g7e.48xlarge |
| GPUs | 8x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120, 96GB GDDR7) |
| VRAM | ~84 GB / 98 GB per GPU (model + KV cache) |
| SGLang | 0.0.0.dev1+g462267982 (nightly cu13 20260219) |
| Triton | 3.5.1 |
| PyTorch | 2.9.1+cu130 |
| CUDA | 13.0 |
| Driver | 580.126.09 |
| OS | Ubuntu 22.04 (kernel 6.8.0-1046-aws) |
| Container | lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20260219-46226798 |

> **Note:** This is a nightly dev build, not a stable release. Pinned to this specific image SHA for reproducibility.

## SM120 Backend Compatibility Matrix

The 122B has DeltaNet linear attention layers (36 of 48 layers), which adds constraints beyond what standard MoE models like M2.5 face on SM120.

| Component | Backend | SM120 Status | Error / Notes |
|-----------|---------|:------------:|---------------|
| FP8 GEMM | DeepGemm | FAIL | `kernel_runtime.hpp:45` assert |
| FP8 GEMM | CUTLASS | FAIL | SM100/SM90-only gate |
| FP8 GEMM | **Triton** | **WORKS** | No SM-specific gate hit |
| Attention | FlashInfer | FAIL on 122B | DeltaNet layers not supported (model arch constraint, not SM120-specific) |
| Attention | **Triton** | **WORKS** | Required for DeltaNet |
| MoE runner | **Triton** | **WORKS** | Only option on SM120 |
| KV cache | fp8_e4m3 | FAIL | Garbage output — no crash, just wrong answers (works on M2.5 @ 0.5.8.post1 and 397B @ same nightly) |
| KV cache | **bf16** | **WORKS** | Required for 122B on SM120 |
| CUDA graphs | — | FAIL | Triton SMEM overflow (106KB > 101KB SM120 limit; PR #17908) |
| HiCache | — | FAIL | DeltaNet incompatible (`HiRadixCache only supports MHA and MLA`) |
| DeepEP | — | FAIL | PCIe P2P topology (g7e has PIX-only pairs) |
| MTP (NextN) | — | **WORKS** | 2.75x single-request speedup |

**Key difference from M2.5:** M2.5 needed `--fp8-gemm-backend triton --moe-runner-backend triton`. The 122B needs those PLUS `--attention-backend triton --kv-cache-dtype bf16 --disable-cuda-graph --disable-radix-cache`. DeltaNet layers add constraints M2.5 didn't have.

## Repro

```bash
SGLANG_DISABLE_DEEP_GEMM=1 \
docker run --gpus all --ipc=host --network host \
  -v /mnt/efs/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20260219-46226798 \
  python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 \
    --tp-size 8 \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
    --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
    --fp8-gemm-backend triton \
    --moe-runner-backend triton \
    --attention-backend triton \
    --disable-cuda-graph \
    --disable-radix-cache \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
    --context-length 131072 \
    --speculative-algo NEXTN \
    --speculative-num-steps 3 \
    --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
    --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4
```

Startup: ~2.5 min with cached weights on EFS. Weight loading: 120s for 39 safetensors shards. Max tokens allocated: 4,916,643 (context_len=131072 sets the upper bound; benchmark prompts use shorter sequences).

## Benchmark Commands

All throughput numbers below come from `sglang.bench_serving`. Exact commands to reproduce:

```bash
# Burst 200in/200out (500 prompts, 3 runs)
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 200 --random-output-len 200 \
  --num-prompts 500 --seed 1 --output-file burst_200_run1.jsonl

# Online 4 req/s (300 prompts, 3 runs)
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 200 --random-output-len 200 \
  --num-prompts 300 --request-rate 4 --seed 1 --output-file online_4rps_run1.jsonl

# Online 8 req/s (300 prompts, 3 runs)
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 200 --random-output-len 200 \
  --num-prompts 300 --request-rate 8 --seed 1 --output-file online_8rps_run1.jsonl

# Long-context 16K input (4 req/s, 3 runs)
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 16384 --random-output-len 256 \
  --num-prompts 100 --request-rate 4 --seed 1 --output-file longctx_16384_4rps_run1.jsonl
```

## Results — Throughput

All runs use `bench_serving` with `--seed 1`. 3-run mean ± std (runs 2-3 for warm; all 3 for long-context).

| Scenario | Output tok/s | Mean TTFT (ms) | P99 TTFT (ms) | Mean ITL (ms) | P99 ITL (ms) | Notes |
|----------|-------------|----------------|---------------|---------------|--------------|-------|
| Burst 200in/200out | **1,985 ± 11** | 2,237 | 3,290 | 123 | 320 | 500 prompts |
| Online 4 req/s | 310 ± 0.3 | 328 | 526 | 173 | 679 | 300 prompts |
| Online 8 req/s | 514 ± 1.7 | 326 | 579 | 206 | 1,178 | P99 ITL spike |
| Long-context 16K in | 209 ± 0.1 | 26,677 | 55,259 | 724 | — | No HiCache |
| Cold-start burst (run 1) | 1,962 | 2,233 | 3,363 | 125 | 261 | Before warmup; mitigation: 50-prompt warmup pass |

## Results — MTP (Multi-Token Prediction)

Of the optimization paths I tested, MTP was the only one that materially improved 122B on SM120. These MTP measurements are single-request manual decode checks, not directly comparable to the `bench_serving` aggregate throughput numbers above.

| Config | tok/s | Speedup | Method |
|--------|-------|---------|--------|
| Baseline (no MTP) | ~9.0 | 1.0x | Manual curl (512 tok / 56.8s) |
| **MTP enabled** | **~25** | **2.75x** | Manual curl (512 tok / ~20s) |

MTP stats under 8-concurrent load (from server logs during nvidia-smi capture):
- Aggregate decode: 140–176 tok/s
- Accept rate: 0.63–0.81 (avg 0.72)
- Accept length: 2.53–3.26 tokens/step
- `max_running_requests` auto-capped to 48 by SGLang for speculative decoding

MTP config: `--speculative-algo NEXTN --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4`

## Results — Quality (Arena-Hard-Auto)

I ran the full Arena-Hard-Auto question set to measure output quality alongside throughput. **Note:** I used Claude Opus 4.6 as the judge model (not GPT-4 as in the original Arena-Hard). Scores are not directly comparable to published Arena-Hard leaderboards — this is a relative comparison between two models using the same judge and same scoring criteria.

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Questions scored | 500/500 (0 errors) |
| Mean score | **6.99/10** (std: 2.58) |
| Median score | 8.0/10 |
| Range | 1.0–10.0 |
| Judge | Claude Opus 4.6 via Bedrock |
| Config | max_tokens=4096, concurrency=8, MTP enabled |
| Runtime | 228.6 min |

Score distribution: 9/10 dominates (193/500, 39%). Bimodal tail — 75 scores at 1–3 (15%) where thinking/reasoning exhausts the token budget before producing an answer.

**Comparison:** M2.5 scored **4.94/10** on the same benchmark with the same judge. The 122B's thinking/reasoning capability drives a +2.05 point quality gap.

## Reference: M2.5 on Same Hardware

For context, here are M2.5 numbers on the same g7e.48xlarge (from [#18870](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/18870)). **Caveat:** M2.5 ran on SGLang 0.5.8.post1 stable; 122B on nightly dev — version differences may affect comparison.

| Dimension | M2.5 | Qwen3.5-122B | Delta |
|-----------|------|-------------|-------|
| Burst tok/s | 1,818 | **1,985** | +9% |
| Online 4 rps | **404** | 310 | -23% |
| Online 8 rps | **744** | 514 | -31% |
| Long-ctx 16K | **404** (warm) | 209 | -48% (HiCache vs none) |
| Single-req tok/s | **72** | 25 (MTP) | -65% |
| Arena-Hard (same judge) | 4.94/10 | **6.99/10** | +42% |
| SM120 optimizations available | FP8 KV, CUDA graphs, HiCache | MTP only | — |

The 122B wins burst throughput and quality. M2.5 wins every sustained serving metric on this hardware, largely because it has access to FP8 KV, CUDA graphs, and HiCache — all blocked on 122B by DeltaNet architecture constraints.

```

Memory: 84–85 GB / 98 GB per GPU (86%). Power: 101–117W / 600W TDP (~18%). Temps: 26–28C.

## Gotchas

1. **FP8 KV cache produced corrupt output silently in this setup.** No crash, no explicit error. Just wrong answers (exclamation marks, repetition). Only detectable by checking output quality. I did not observe the same failure on M2.5 (0.5.8.post1) or Qwen3.5-397B (same nightly) under their tested configs. Suspected cause: DeltaNet linear attention state interacting poorly with fp8-quantized KV at the smaller hidden dim (3072 vs 4096). `bf16` KV was the workaround.

2. **DeltaNet attention backend behavior may not be obvious from current docs.** FlashInfer failed on the 36 DeltaNet layers in my testing, so `--attention-backend triton` was required.

3. **MTP `max_running_requests` auto-capped to 48.** SGLang's speculative decoding path limits concurrency. Logged as a startup warning but easy to miss.

4. **HiCache is completely blocked.** Not just degraded. DeltaNet layers trigger `HiRadixCache only supports MHA and MLA` error. This means no prefix caching for long-context workloads.

5. **Nightly build required.** The container image (`nightly-dev-cu13-20260219-46226798`) is not a stable release. Pin the exact SHA for reproducibility.

## Key Takeaways

1. **DeltaNet models need more SM120 workarounds than standard MoE.** M2.5 needed 2 triton backend flags. The 122B needs those plus attention backend, KV dtype override, and no CUDA graphs — 6 flags total to get a working server.

2. **Of the optimization paths I tested, MTP was the only one that improved performance.** 2.75x single-request speedup (~9 to ~25 tok/s). Accept rate averages 0.72, meaning ~3 tokens per speculative step.

3. **FP8 KV cache failure is model-specific.** Works on M2.5, broken on 122B with no crash or error — only detectable by checking output quality. May be DeltaNet-related (linear attention state + fp8 quantization at 3072 hidden dim). PR #18904 may fix the underlying dequant scale bug.

4. **Burst throughput doesn't predict sustained serving.** 122B beats M2.5 on burst (+9%) but loses on every online serving metric in my tests. Burst is a misleading proxy for production readiness.

5. **Quality (6.99 vs 4.94 Arena-Hard) comes at a serving cost.** Arena-Hard averaged ~27s per question at concurrency=8; single complex requests took ~3 min at MTP-enabled single-request throughput (~25 tok/s × 4096 max tokens). The quality gap is real but so is the latency gap.

6. **On this hardware and methodology, M2.5 remains the better production-serving fit.** 122B's DeltaNet architecture blocks too many SM120 optimizations for competitive sustained throughput today.

## Proof

candidates.title: [Performance Regression] ~2x throughput drop in disaggregated PD mode with Wide-EP (DeepSeek-R1 FP4, GB200) between SGLang v0.5.8 and latest nightly
candidates.body:
## Summary

We observed a significant performance regression in **Wide-EP prefill-decode disaggregated serving** for DeepSeek-R1 (FP4, GB200 NVL72) between SGLang `v0.5.8` (Jan 2026) and the `dev` container (April 1 2026) (The issue should be already existing with sglang-TOT 3.18 according to @nvcastet). At high concurrency (≥2048), throughput drops by ~2x and TTFT increases dramatically. We include detailed worker-level log metrics below for further analysis.

## Environment

- **Hardware**: NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 (partition `gb200`, 12 nodes: 4 prefill + 8 decode, 48 GPUs total)
- **Model**: DeepSeek-R1, FP4 quantization (`modelopt_fp4`), `kv-cache-dtype: fp8_e4m3`, `attention-backend: trtllm_mla`
- **Disaggregation**: Prefill-Decode disagg with NIXL transfer backend
- **Prefill**: TP=4, DP=4, EP=4 per node (4 workers, 1 per node)
- **Decode**: TP=32, DP=32, EP=32 across 8 nodes (1 worker spanning all 8 nodes)
- **Frontend**: Dynamo with 10 frontends (1 + 9 additional), NGINX load balancer
- **Benchmark**: `sa-bench`, ISL=1024, OSL=1024, concurrencies 512/2048/4096/8192

## Baseline Data

@nvcastet  provided two benchmark runs with identical hardware and config, differing only in SGLang/Dynamo version:

### "Good" Run — SGLang v0.5.8 + Dynamo 0.8.1 (2026-03-12)

- Container: `dev-sglang:v0.5.8-cu130.sqsh`
- Dynamo: 0.8.1

| Concurrency | Output Throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Mean ITL (ms) | Mean E2EL (ms) |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------|----------------|---------------|-----------------|
| 512         | **33,070**               | **856**        | 13.96          | 680           | 13,720          |
| 2048        | **106,783**              | **1,301**      | 16.99          | 828           | 16,955          |
| 4096        | **151,238**              | **4,560**      | 21.23          | 1,034         | 24,096          |
| 8192        | **138,218**              | **32,847**     | 21.79          | 1,061         | 52,904          |

### "Bad" Run — SGLang `dev-0318` + Dynamo 1.0.0 (2026-03-30)

- Container: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev` (around Mar 18 nightly dev build with a perf fix: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/21771)
- Dynamo: 1.0.0 (installed via `dynamo.sh` setup script, `ai_dynamo-1.0.0` and some fixes)

| Concurrency | Output Throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Mean ITL (ms) | Mean E2EL (ms) |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------|----------------|---------------|-----------------|
| 512         | 32,458                   | 924            | 14.15          | 689           | 13,962          |
| 2048        | 72,635 (**-32%**)        | 10,215 (**+7.9x**) | 15.69     | 764           | 24,673          |
| 4096        | 74,379 (**-51%**)        | 33,648 (**+7.4x**) | 15.84     | 771           | 48,226          |
| 8192        | 75,507 (**-45%**)        | 80,042 (**+2.4x**) | 16.07     | 783           | 94,839          |

**Key observation**: At concurrency ≥2048, throughput is cut roughly in half and TTFT explodes. At concurrency=512 performance is similar, suggesting the issue is related to scheduling/transfer under load, not raw compute.

## Reproduction Results

We reproduced using the same recipe config on the same hardware.

### Run 1: SGLang `dev-0401` (nightly Apr 1) + Dynamo source `38b9936` (≈1.0.0+)

Our verification run using a more recent nightly container (`dev-0401`, Apr 1). Results closely track Nicolas's "bad" (`dev-0318`) numbers, confirming the regression persists:

| Concurrency | Output Throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------|----------------|
| 512         | 28,861                   | 1,854          | 14.18          |
| 2048        | 63,699                   | 11,058         | 15.57          |
| 4096        | 69,767                   | 31,161         | 15.95          |
| 8192        | 72,335                   | 73,302         | 15.95          |

### Run 2: SGLang `v0.5.8` + Dynamo `0.8.1` (pip)

Exact version match with Nicolas's "good" setup. **Performance matches the "good" baseline**:

| Concurrency | Output Throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------|----------------|
| 512         | 29,796                   | 1,873          | 14.03          |
| 2048        | 88,601                   | 2,843          | 17.71          |
| 4096        | 131,592                  | 5,285          | 22.25          |
| 8192        | 154,354                  | 21,687         | 23.58          |

### Run 3: SGLang `dev-0401` + Dynamo source + Mooncake transfer backend

Tried switching `disaggregation-transfer-backend: mooncake` to rule out NIXL-specific issues. Results are similar to Run 1 (NIXL), no improvement:

| Concurrency | Output Throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Mean ITL (ms) | Mean E2EL (ms) |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------|----------------|---------------|-----------------|
| 512         | 28,784                   | 1,856          | 14.20          | 692           | 14,945          |
| 2048        | 63,304                   | 11,365         | 15.63          | 761           | 25,763          |
| 4096        | 68,865                   | 31,827         | 15.86          | 772           | 46,435          |
| 8192        | 72,227                   | 73,570         | 16.04          | 781           | 88,338          |

Mooncake prefill logs show even higher `#inflight-req` (27-30) and `token usage` (0.32-0.35) compared to NIXL Run 1 (17-18 and 0.25-0.26). Decode `gen throughput` and `#running-req` are comparable to Run 1 (~2,400-2,550 tok/s, 35-43 running).

## Worker-Level Log Metrics Comparison

We extracted detailed per-worker metrics from our own reproduction runs (Run 1: `dev-0401` and Run 2: `v0.5.8`) during steady-state (concurrency=4096 phase) to compare behavior.

### Prefill Worker Logs

**v0.5.8 (good)**:
```

Note: The prefill side actually shows *higher* raw input throughput in the bad case, while `#inflight-req` remains persistently at 17-18 (vs 0 in the good case). The `token usage` is also 2x higher in the bad case.

### Decode Worker Logs

**v0.5.8 (good)**:
```

**dev-0401 (bad)**:
```
Decode batch, #running-req: 40, #token: 212096, token usage: 0.07, #transfer-req: 165, gen throughput: 2,588 tok/s

Decode batch, #running-req: 36, #token:  51712, token usage: 0.02, #transfer-req:   2, gen throughput: 2,368 tok/s
```

| Metric | v0.5.8 (good) | dev-0401 (bad) |
|--------|---------------|----------------|
| `#running-req` | **77-166** | **36-44** (~3-4x fewer) |
| `gen throughput` (per DP shard) | **4,997-5,874 tok/s** | **2,368-2,588 tok/s** (~2.3x lower) |
| `#transfer-req` (peak) | 132 → drains to 0 | 165 → drains slower |
| `token usage` | 0.04-0.10 | 0.02-0.07 |

## Bisection Attempts

We attempted to bisect the regression window between v0.5.8 (Jan 23) and dev-0401 (Apr 1):

| SGLang Version | Release Date | Dynamo Version | Result |
|----------------|-------------|----------------|--------|
| **v0.5.8**     | Jan 23      | 0.8.1          | ✅ Good performance |
| nightly-0213   | Feb 13      | 0.9.0          | ❌ `Overflow when unpacking long long` in `disaggregation/utils.py:set_buf` |
| nightly-0213   | Feb 13      | 0.9.1          | ❌ Same overflow error |
| nightly-0213   | Feb 13      | 1.0.0          | ❌ `Engine.async_generate() got unexpected keyword argument 'return_routed_experts'` |
| **v0.5.9**     | Feb 24      | 0.8.1          | ❌ NATS routing broken (requests never reach workers) |
| v0.5.9         | Feb 24      | 0.9.0          | ❌ NATS routing broken |
| v0.5.9         | Feb 24      | 0.9.1          | ❌ NATS routing broken |
| v0.5.9         | Feb 24      | **1.0.0**      | ✅ Runs but prefill worker crashed mid-benchmark (TRT-LLM cutlass kernel error) |
| **dev-0401**   | Apr 1       | source (≈1.0.0+) | ✅ Runs but **degraded performance** (≈Nicolas "bad") |

**Findings**:
- SGLang v0.5.9 requires Dynamo ≥1.0.0 to even route requests (NATS protocol change)
- The `nightly-0213` container is incompatible with all available Dynamo versions
- The regression window is between **v0.5.8 (Jan 23)** and **v0.5.9 (Feb 24)**, approximately 1 month

## Discussion

Notable observations from the worker-level metrics:

1. **Prefill `#inflight-req`**: Persistently 17-18 in the bad case vs 0 in the good case. This indicates that in the bad case, completed prefill requests are waiting rather than being immediately handed off.

2. **Prefill `token usage`**: 2x higher in the bad case (0.25-0.26 vs 0.12-0.13), consistent with more KV data being held in prefill worker memory (i.e., completed prefills not yet transferred out).

3. **Prefill `input throughput`**: Actually *higher* in the bad case (19,500-20,100 vs 12,100-14,800 tok/s). The prefill compute itself appears faster or at least comparable.

4. **Decode `#running-req`**: Only 36-44 in the bad case vs 77-166 in the good case. The decode worker has far fewer active requests generating tokens.

5. **Decode `gen throughput`**: ~2,400-2,600 tok/s in the bad case vs ~5,000-5,800 tok/s in the good case (per-DP-shard). The lower running request count directly reduces decode throughput.

6. **Transfer backend**: Switching from NIXL to Mooncake did not improve the situation, suggesting the bottleneck is not specific to the transfer backend implementation.

7. **Concurrency dependence**: At concurrency=512, performance is similar between good and bad. The degradation appears at concurrency ≥2048, suggesting the issue is related to behavior under high load rather than per-request overhead.

These metrics point to a change somewhere in the disaggregation data path between SGLang v0.5.8 (Jan 23) and v0.5.9 (Feb 24). The exact root cause has not been identified. Possible areas to investigate:
- Changes to `sglang/srt/disaggregation/` between Jan 23 and Feb 24
- KV transfer scheduling or queuing logic
- Prefill-to-decode handoff mechanism
- Connection management under high concurrency

<!-- ## Additional Issue: `sa-bench` Tokenizer Bug (Separate, Fixed)

During initial debugging, we discovered that `sa-bench` (the benchmark client) was generating inflated token counts for DeepSeek-R1 due to a `transformers` v5 bug: `LlamaTokenizerFast` overwrites the true `ByteLevel` pre_tokenizer for DeepSeek-R1, causing ~6x token inflation (6116 tokens for a 1024-token prompt). This was fixed by porting SGLang's `_fix_v5_tokenizer_components()` to `sa-bench`. **This is a client-side bug only and does not affect the performance regression.** -->

## Setup Details

### Recipe Config (YAML)

```yaml
model:
  path: dsfp4                    # DeepSeek-R1 FP4 checkpoint
  precision: fp4

resources:
  gpu_type: gb200
  prefill_nodes: 4
  decode_nodes: 8
  prefill_workers: 4             # 1 per prefill node
  decode_workers: 1              # 1 spanning all 8 decode nodes
  gpus_per_node: 4

frontend:
  type: dynamo
  enable_multiple_frontends: true
  num_additional_frontends: 9    # 10 total frontends
  nginx_container: nginx

backend:
  sglang_config:
    prefill:
      tp-size: 4
      dp-size: 4
      ep-size: 4
      attention-backend: trtllm_mla
      quantization: modelopt_fp4
      kv-cache-dtype: fp8_e4m3
      disaggregation-mode: prefill
      disaggregation-transfer-backend: nixl
      mem-fraction-static: 0.84
      max-total-tokens: 131072
      max-prefill-tokens: 32768
      chunked-prefill-size: 65536
      disable-cuda-graph: true
      enable-dp-attention: true
      enable-single-batch-overlap: true
      disable-radix-cache: true

    decode:
      tp-size: 32
      dp-size: 32
      ep-size: 32
      attention-backend: trtllm_mla
      quantization: modelopt_fp4
      kv-cache-dtype: fp8_e4m3
      disaggregation-mode: decode
      disaggregation-transfer-backend: nixl
      mem-fraction-static: 0.83
      max-total-tokens: 3122380
      max-running-requests: 67584
      moe-a2a-backend: deepep
      deepep-mode: low_latency
      ep-dispatch-algorithm: static
      ep-num-redundant-experts: 32
      enable-dp-attention: true
      enable-dp-lm-head: true

benchmark:
  type: sa-bench
  isl: 1024
  osl: 1024
  concurrencies: 512x2048x4096x8192
  req_rate: inf
```

### Key Environment Variables

```
SGLANG_NVFP4_CKPT_FP8_GEMM_IN_ATTN=1
SGLANG_PER_TOKEN_GROUP_QUANT_8BIT_V2=1
SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_HEARTBEAT_MAX_FAILURE=100000
SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT=100000
SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_WAITING_TIMEOUT=100000
SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL=True
SGLANG_USE_MESSAGE_QUEUE_BROADCASTER=0
SGLANG_DISABLE_TP_MEMORY_INBALANCE_CHECK=1
# Decode-only:
SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK=1024
SGLANG_MOE_NVFP4_DISPATCH=1
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use the recipe config above with SGLang `v0.5.8` container + Dynamo `0.8.1` → observe good performance
2. Use the same config with SGLang `dev-0401` (or any recent nightly) + latest Dynamo → observe ~2x throughput drop at concurrency ≥2048
3. Check decode worker logs for `#transfer-req` — it will be high (15-20+) in the bad case vs 0-1 in the good case

## Expected vs Actual

- **Expected**: Performance should be at least as good as v0.5.8 (or better with optimizations)
- **Actual**: ~2x throughput regression at high concurrency, ~8x TTFT increase at concurrency=2048

candidates.title: Quality regression (LLM-as-judge scores) after upgrading from 0.5.9 to 0.5.10rc0 with Qwen3.5-27B-FP8 on Blackwell SM120
candidates.body:
After upgrading from sglang 0.5.9 to 0.5.10rc0, I'm observing a significant quality regression when serving Qwen3.5-27B-FP8. ## Description

During piecewise CUDA graph warmup compilation for `lmsys/gpt-oss-120b-bf16` (4-GPU) on B200, a segmentation fault occurs in the Triton NVIDIA driver backend while executing the fused MoE experts kernel.

The crash happens at ~93% of the "Compiling num tokens" phase (69/74 iterations).

## Error Stack Trace

  ...

```

## Environment

- **GPU**: NVIDIA B200
- **Model**: `lmsys/gpt-oss-120b-bf16` (TP=4)
- **Attention backend**: `trtllm_mha`
- **CI job**: `stage-c-test-4-gpu-b200 (0)` in [PR Test run](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/23680918199/attempts/7?pr=19915)

## Analysis

The segfault originates in the Triton NVIDIA driver backend (`triton/backends/nvidia/driver.py:668`) during JIT compilation/execution of the MoE `matmul_ogs` kernel. This appears to be a Triton + B200 (SM100) driver-level issue during CUDA graph warmup.

candidates.title: [Bug] Eagle V2 speculative decoding crashes with NaN in logits when radix cache prefix hit occurs (SM120 / 8 * RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell)
candidates.body:
## Environment

| Component | Version |
|-----------|---------|
| Container | `lmsysorg/sglang:glm5-blackwell` (sha256:968b8bc5f67c) |
| Model | [festr2/GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP](https://huggingface.co/festr2/GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP) |
| GPU | 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96GB (SM120, TP=8) |
| CUDA | 12.9.1 |
| Quantization | modelopt_fp4 |
| KV cache dtype | bfloat16 (auto-set by server_args.py for DSA on SM12) |
| Speculative algorithm | NEXTN (mapped to EAGLE / eagle_worker_v2) |

## Launch command
```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /model \
  --served-model-name GLM-5 \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --kv-cache-dtype auto \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --attention-backend flashinfer \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass \
  --disable-custom-all-reduce \
  --enable-flashinfer-allreduce-fusion \
  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \
  --speculative-num-steps 1 \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 1 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --reasoning-parser glm45 \
  --tool-call-parser glm47 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.92 \
  --max-running-requests 8 \
  --enable-nan-detection \
  --watchdog-timeout 600
```
(env: `SGLANG_ENABLE_SPEC_V2=True`, `SGLANG_ENABLE_JIT_DEEPGEMM=0`, `SGLANG_ENABLE_DEEP_GEMM=0`)

## Bug description

Server starts successfully, CUDA graphs captured, speculative decoding works fine on the **first requests** (accept rate ~0.85–0.94, ~50 tok/s).

Crash occurs **consistently** when a subsequent request hits the **radix cache prefix** (`#cached-token > 0`). On the first such request, `eagle_worker_v2.py` raises `NaN in the logits` and all TP workers crash simultaneously.

## Crash traceback
```
[2026-03-03 18:14:33 TP1] Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 3076, in run_scheduler_process
    scheduler.event_loop_overlap()
  File ".../scheduler.py", line 1123, in event_loop_overlap
    batch_result = self.run_batch(batch)
  File ".../scheduler.py", line 2279, in run_batch
    batch_result = self.model_worker.forward_batch_generation(...)
  File ".../sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py", line 675, in forward_batch_generation
    batch_output = self.verify(model_worker_batch)
  File ".../sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py", line 765, in verify
    detect_nan(logits_output)
  File ".../sglang/srt/speculative/spec_utils.py", line 713, in detect_nan
    raise ValueError("Detected errors during sampling! NaN in the logits.")
ValueError: Detected errors during sampling! NaN in the logits.
```
(all 8 TP workers crash at the same timestamp)

## Reproduction pattern

The crash is **100% reproducible** with this sequence:

1. Send request A (input ~200 tokens) → completes normally, accept_rate ~0.9
2. Send request B (input ~3000 tokens, no cache overlap) → completes normally
3. Send request C (input ~4400 tokens, **overlaps with previous context → `#cached-token=2688`**) → **crash on step 2 of decode**

Log line immediately before crash:
```
Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 1792, #cached-token: 2688, ...
Decode batch, #running-req: 1, #token: 4480, accept len: 1.82, accept rate: 0.91, ...
Decode batch, #running-req: 1, #token: 4544, accept len: 1.75, accept rate: 0.88, ...
→ CRASH
```

## Key observation

**Without speculative decoding** (same hardware, same model, same NSA patches) the server is fully stable:
- Handled 15,000+ token contexts without issues
- No NaN, no crashes across dozens of requests

This strongly suggests the bug is in **Eagle V2 verify path when processing a batch where KV cache was partially populated from radix cache prefix**, not in the base model or attention backend.

## Additional context

- SM120 (Blackwell) requires several patches to run GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP:
  - KV cache dtype forced to bfloat16 (fp8_e4m3 unsupported for DSA on SM12)
  - NSA backends patched from `flashmla_sparse`/`trtllm` → `flashinfer` (SM90/SM100-only backends produce NaN on SM120)
  - DeepGemm disabled (`SGLANG_ENABLE_JIT_DEEPGEMM=0`, `SGLANG_ENABLE_DEEP_GEMM=0`) — separate numerical instability issue on Blackwell
- `speculative_algorithm` is set to `NEXTN` in CLI but gets mapped to `EAGLE` internally with `draft_model_path = target_model_path` (MTP heads reused)
- `SGLANG_ENABLE_SPEC_V2=True` is required, otherwise NEXTN falls back silently to non-v2 Eagle and loads the full model twice → OOM

## Workaround

Disabling speculative decoding entirely resolves the crash. Running without MTP: **~33 tok/s**. With MTP (before crash): **~50 tok/s**, accept_rate 0.80–0.94.

Would be happy to provide full logs or test patches. This hardware (SM120) is fully available for testing.

candidates.title: [Bug] NVFP4 models produce NaN outputs on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120)
candidates.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Running NVFP4 quantized models (e.g., `vincentzed-hf/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4`) on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120) produces NaN outputs and garbage generation.

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path vincentzed-hf/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4 \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --port 8000 \
  --attention-backend triton \
  --fp4-gemm-backend flashinfer_cutlass
```
```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "qwen3.5", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}], "max_tokens": 50}'
```

**Result:** NaN in logits, model outputs garbage

### Environment

| Component | Version |
|-----------|---------|
| GPU | NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (8x, 96GB each) |
| Compute Capability | SM 12.0 |
| SGLang | 0.4.7+ (vz/qwen3-5 branch) |
| FlashInfer | 0.6.3 |
| CUDA | 13 |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04 |

candidates.title: NaN in hidden states with modelopt_fp4 quantization under concurrent load (GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP on Blackwell)
candidates.body:
## Summary

GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP with `--quantization modelopt_fp4` produces **NaN values in model hidden states** under concurrent request load, causing `torch.multinomial` to crash with `probability tensor contains either inf, nan or element < 0`. 

This is **not** related to speculative decoding, radix cache, or any specific attention backend — the NaN originates directly from the model's transformer layers.

## Environment

- **Hardware**: 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120, 96GB each)
- **Model**: GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP (`--quantization modelopt_fp4`)
- **SGLang**: Built from `main` (commit `346a4131cfbac5`)
- **PyTorch**: 2.7+ (nightly, Blackwell support)
- **Docker**: Custom image based on `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.03-py3`
- **CUDA**: 12.8+

## Launch command

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /mnt/GLM-5-NVFP4-MTP \
  --tp 8 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --attention-backend flashinfer \
  --moe-runner-backend cutlass \
  --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --disable-custom-all-reduce \
  --enable-flashinfer-allreduce-fusion \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.88 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs 32 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5000 \
  --served-model-name glm-5 \
  --max-running-requests 64 \
  --enable-metrics
```

## Reproducer

The bug requires **concurrent requests** — serial requests don't trigger it. Save this as `test_nan_concurrent.py`:

```python
"""
Concurrent reproducer for NaN crash with modelopt_fp4 quantization.

Sends bursts of 64 concurrent requests with a shared prefix.
Typically crashes within 2-5 rounds without --enable-nan-detection.

Usage:
    python3 test_nan_concurrent.py --url http://localhost:5000 --concurrency 64
"""

import argparse, json, sys, time, requests
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

def send(base, prefix, suffix, model, i):
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prefix + suffix}],
        "max_tokens": 64,
        "temperature": 0.7,
    }
    try:
        r = requests.post(f"{base}/v1/chat/completions", json=payload, timeout=180)
        r.raise_for_status()
        return i, True, ""
    except Exception as e:
        return i, False, str(e)[:200]

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--url", default="http://localhost:5000")
    parser.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--rounds", type=int, default=0, help="0=infinite")
    parser.add_argument("--model", default="glm-5")
    parser.add_argument("--prefix-repeat", type=int, default=60)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    prefix = (
        "You are an expert assistant specializing in science, technology, "
        "and history. You provide detailed, accurate, and well-structured "
        "answers. Always cite relevant facts and provide context. "
    ) * args.prefix_repeat

    suffixes = [
        "Explain the theory of general relativity in simple terms.",
        "What caused the fall of the Roman Empire?",
        "How do mRNA vaccines work?",
        "Describe the process of nuclear fusion in stars.",
        "What are the main differences between TCP and UDP?",
        "Explain quantum entanglement to a 10-year-old.",
        "What is the significance of the Turing test?",
        "How does photosynthesis work at the molecular level?",
    ]

    # Flush cache and seed
    try:
        requests.post(f"{args.url}/flush_cache", timeout=30)
    except:
        pass
    time.sleep(0.5)
    send(args.url, prefix, "Say hello.", args.model, 0)
    print(f"Running bursts of {args.concurrency} concurrent requests...")

    rnd = 0
    max_rounds = args.rounds if args.rounds > 0 else float("inf")
    t0 = time.monotonic()

    while rnd < max_rounds:
        rnd += 1
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.concurrency) as pool:
            futs = [
                pool.submit(send, args.url, prefix, suffixes[i % len(suffixes)], args.model, i)
                for i in range(args.concurrency)
            ]
            fails = sum(1 for f in as_completed(futs) if not f.result()[1])
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
        if fails:
            print(f"Round {rnd}: {fails}/{args.concurrency} FAILED after {elapsed:.0f}s")
            print("Check server logs for NaN tracebacks.")
            sys.exit(1)
        if rnd % 10 == 0:
            print(f"Round {rnd}: OK ({elapsed:.0f}s)")

    print(f"Completed {rnd} rounds without crash in {time.monotonic()-t0:.0f}s")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Run: `python3 test_nan_concurrent.py --url http://localhost:5000 --concurrency 64`

## Crash traceback

```
/pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/TensorCompare.cu:109: _assert_async_cuda_kernel: block: [0,0,0], thread: [0,0,0]
Assertion `probability tensor contains either `inf`, `nan` or element < 0` failed.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "scheduler.py", line 1211, in event_loop_overlap
    batch_result = self.run_batch(batch)
  File "scheduler.py", line 2370, in run_batch
    batch_result = self.model_worker.forward_batch_generation(...)
  File "tp_worker.py", line 500, in forward_batch_generation
    batch_result.next_token_ids = self.model_runner.sample(...)
  File "model_runner.py", line 2570, in sample
    next_token_ids = self.sampler(...)
  File "sampler.py", line 161, in forward
    batch_next_token_ids = self._sample_from_probs(...)
  File "sampler.py", line 202, in _sample_from_probs
    batch_next_token_ids = sampling_from_probs_torch(...)
  File "sampler.py", line 600, in sampling_from_probs_torch
    sampled_index = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered
```

## Root cause analysis

We instrumented the code with synchronous NaN checks at multiple stages to trace exactly where NaN originates:

### 1. NaN comes from model hidden_states, NOT from sampling/softmax

We added a NaN check in `DeepseekV2ForCausalLM.forward()` (which `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM` inherits) before `logits_processor`:

```
!!! DS_MODEL hidden_states NaN before logits_processor: 1007616/7403520 elements, shape=torch.Size([1205, 6144])
```

**~13.6% of hidden state elements are NaN** in affected batches. This is not a single-token numerical edge case — entire sequences within the batch have NaN hidden states.

### 2. NaN propagates through the pipeline

```
hidden_states (NaN) → lm_head matmul → logits (NaN) → softmax → probs (NaN) → multinomial → CRASH
```

### 3. It's NOT related to speculative decoding

Crash reproduces identically **without** any speculative decoding args (`--speculative-eagle-model` etc. removed).

### 4. It's NOT related to radix cache

Crash reproduces with `--disable-radix-cache`.

### 5. High concurrency is required

- **Serial requests**: 50+ rounds, no crash
- **8 concurrent**: Crashes after ~5 runs of the reproducer
- **64 concurrent**: Crashes within 2-5 rounds consistently

This suggests the NaN may be related to batch size / memory access patterns rather than a cache race condition.

### 6. `--enable-nan-detection` is an effective workaround

With `--enable-nan-detection`, the sampler replaces NaN logits with `-1e5` (effectively zero probability after softmax). The affected tokens are simply not selected.

**Stress test result with `--enable-nan-detection`:**
- 200 rounds × 64 concurrent requests = **12,800 requests over 21 minutes — ZERO crashes**
- 3,136 NaN detections were logged during this run (NaN still occurs but is handled gracefully)

## What we investigated (not the cause)

| Hypothesis | Result |
|---|---|
| Speculative decoding (EAGLE-v2) | ❌ Crashes without spec decoding |
| Radix cache prefix hit race | ❌ Crashes with `--disable-radix-cache` |
| Softmax numerical instability | ❌ NaN already present before softmax |
| Temperature division by zero | ❌ Temperature is 0.7 (valid) |
| top_k/top_p renormalization | ❌ NaN present before these are called |
| `SGLANG_SPEC_NAN_DETECTION=1` | ⚠️ Uses `torch._assert_async` — same generic CUDA assert message, doesn't help isolate the source |

## Likely root cause

The NaN originates in the **transformer layers** of the model with `modelopt_fp4` quantization. With 13.6% of hidden state elements being NaN in affected batches, this points to:

1. **FP4 dequantization numerical instability** under specific input patterns that only manifest with larger batch sizes
2. **Possible race condition in quantized weight access** when multiple sequences are processed concurrently
3. **Kernel-level issue** in the cutlass MoE runner or attention computation with FP4 weights

## Workaround

Add `--enable-nan-detection` to the launch command. This replaces NaN logits with `-1e5` before sampling, preventing the crash. Quality impact appears minimal since the NaN tokens receive ~0 probability and valid tokens are selected instead.

## Related

- #19796 — Similar NaN crash report (initially attributed to radix cache + EAGLE-v2, but root cause is deeper)
- PR #19897 — Zero-fill draft KV for cached prefix (does not fix this issue)

candidates.title: [Feature] Auto-fallback from DeepGemm when checkpoint scale_fmt is not ue8m0
candidates.body:
### Checklist
- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When SGLang auto-enables DeepGemm on Blackwell and detects that the checkpoint's scale format is not `ue8m0`, it logs a warning but proceeds anyway:

```
WARNING model_config.py: DeepGemm is enabled but the scale_fmt of checkpoint is not ue8m0.
This might cause accuracy degradation on Blackwell.
```

The "accuracy degradation" described in the warning is severe enough to cause **CUDA crashes under load** — `device-side assert triggered` (NaN/Inf in probability tensor) or `illegal instruction` at concurrency ≥ 64.

**Suggested fix:** When `fp4_gemm_runner_backend == 'auto'` and the checkpoint's `scale_fmt != ue8m0`, SGLang should automatically fall back to a non-DeepGemm backend (e.g., `flashinfer_cutlass`) instead of enabling DeepGemm with an incompatible checkpoint. The current warning should be upgraded to an automatic fallback with an info-level log message explaining why DeepGemm was not used.

This class of bug affects multiple models on Blackwell — see #16816, #16595, #20375. In each case users had to manually discover and set `--fp4-gemm-backend` or `--fp8-gemm-backend` as a workaround (which currently doesn't even work for FP4 — see #20775).

### Reproduction

```bash
# Any NVFP4 checkpoint with non-ue8m0 scale format on any Blackwell GPU
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \

candidates.title: [Bug] --fp4-gemm-backend flashinfer_cutlass does not disable DeepGemm on Blackwell
candidates.body:
### Checklist
- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Setting `--fp4-gemm-backend flashinfer_cutlass` does not prevent DeepGemm from being enabled on Blackwell GPUs. The flag is correctly parsed (`fp4_gemm_runner_backend='flashinfer_cutlass'` in server args), but DeepGemm is still activated — the following warning appears 4 times during startup:

```
WARNING model_config.py: DeepGemm is enabled but the scale_fmt of checkpoint is not ue8m0.
This might cause accuracy degradation on Blackwell.
```

Adding `--fp8-gemm-backend triton` also does not suppress DeepGemm.

This means there is **no way to disable DeepGemm via CLI flags** when serving NVFP4 checkpoints on Blackwell, which leads to CUDA crashes at concurrency ≥ 64 when the checkpoint's scale format is not `ue8m0`.

### Reproduction

```bash
# Model: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4 (NVFP4, non-ue8m0 scale format)
# GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (CC 12.0)

# Expected: DeepGemm should NOT be used when --fp4-gemm-backend is set explicitly
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --fp4-gemm-backend flashinfer_cutlass \
  --fp8-gemm-backend triton \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

# Actual: DeepGemm warning still fires 4 times during startup.
# At concurrency >= 64, server crashes with:
#   CUDA error: an illegal instruction was encountered
# or:
#   Assertion `probability tensor contains either `inf`, `nan` or element < 0` failed.
```

Concurrency 1 and 16 complete successfully. The crash is triggered at concurrency 64+ due to accumulated numerical errors from the DeepGemm/scale_fmt mismatch.

Related issues: #16816, #16595

candidates.title: [RFE] Add Reduced-Layers Functional and Accuracy Tests
candidates.body: # [RFE] Add Reduced-Layers Functional and Accuracy Tests Refer to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20514 for the high-level SGLang CI improvement initiative and refer to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20847 for Q2 2026 roadmap. ## Motivation SGLang's current e2e accuracy tests rely on actual accuracy metrics (GSM8K/MMLU/GPQA), either running with large models or smaller proxy lite models (e.g., DeepSeek-V2-Lite for DeepSeek-V3). The problems: - **Large models are slow** — tests take minutes to hours, so we cannot add more configs (parallelism, precisions, flag combinations) to increase coverage. - **Full accuracy metric is slow** — tests that measure the actual accuracy metrics (GSM8K/MMLU/GPQA) are slow due to the size of the validation dataset. However, usually the garbage output issue or functional issues like crashes only need one data sample to repro. - **Lite proxy models lose coverage** — some code paths are hard-coded to only support the hyperparameters of large models (e.g., specific number of experts), so lite models skip those paths. **The solution:** Run with the large model but override `num_hidden_layers` to a small number (e.g., 2), keeping everything else (parallel configs, expert count, etc.) the same. This exploits the fact that LLMs are stacks of identical decoder layers. We get ~30x faster tests while preserving the full model graph and all code paths. In addition, we do not need to run through the entire validation dataset. The proposed test hierarchy will look like: ## Test Design ### Two Sub-Tiers **1. test_sanity — "It runs without crashing"** - Uses `--load-format dummy` (random weights, no download) - Uses `--json-model-override-args '{"num_hidden_layers": 2}'` - Sends a batch of requests, verifies valid responses without errors - Catches: CUDA errors, shape mismatches, wrong assertions, OOM, parallelism config bugs **Example:** ```python class TestDeepSeekR1Sanity(DefaultServerBase): model = "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1" other_args = [ "--load-format", "dummy", "--json-model-override-args", '{"num_hidden_layers": 4, "first_k_dense_replace": 2}', "--trust-remote-code", ] def test_sanity(self): response = send_request(self.base_url, prompt="Hello world") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200) ``` **2. test_allclose_to_hf — "It produces the same output as HuggingFace"** - Creates a tiny HF model with reduced layers and random weights - Launches SGLang with the same checkpoint - Compares output logits with `torch.testing.assert_close()` - Additionally catches: wrong AllReduce/AllGather, missing residual connections, skipped RMSNorm, wrong RoPE config ### Code Coverage Principle What configs to add should be driven by **code coverage**. If TP=4 and TP=8 share identical code paths, only one is needed. But if certain code paths are only triggered for TP=8 (e.g., different communication patterns), both configs should be added to ensure coverage. The goal is to cover all distinct code paths, not all possible parameter values. ## Proposed Test Organization ``` test/registered/reduced_layers/ test_reduced_layers_deepseek_r1.py test_reduced_layers_llama.py test_reduced_layers_qwen3_moe.py test_reduced_layers_qwen35.py test_reduced_layers_glm5.py test_reduced_layers_minimax_m25.py test_reduced_layers_glm47.py test_reduced_layers_qwen3_coder.py ``` ### Configuration Dimensions to Cover | Dimension | Example Values | Why It Matters | |---|---|---| | Tensor Parallel (TP) | 1, 2, 4, 8 | Different AllReduce/AllGather patterns | | Expert Parallel (EP) | 1, 2, 4, 8 | MoE routing + communication | | Pipeline Parallel (EP) | 1, 2, 4, 8 | PP pipelining | | Attention Data Parallel (ADP) | True / False | Attention parallelism strategy | | Precision | bf16, fp8, fp4 | Quantization kernel paths | | Attention Backend | FlashInfer, Triton, FA3 | Different attention implementations | | KV-cache dtype | bf16, fp8, nvfp4 | Different attention implementations | | Chunked Prefill | on / off | Different scheduling paths | | Max Num Tokens | 2048, 4096, 8192 | Memory allocation patterns | | CUDA Graph | on / off | Graph capture/replay correctness | | Speculative Decoding | on / off | Draft model integration | | Context + Generation mixed batch | yes / no | Mixed batch handling | ### Existing Infrastructure The following SGLang features already support this pattern: - `--json-model-override-args '{"num_hidden_layers": 2}'` — already used in tests like `test_dummy_grok_models.py` - `--load-format dummy` — loads random weights, no download needed - `DefaultServerBase` + mixin pattern — clean declarative test setup - `register_cuda_ci()` — CI registration with suite-based partitioning ### Prior Art - **[HuggingFace Transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/tests/models)** — 421+ model test files, each with tiny configs (hidden_size=32, num_hidden_layers=2) - **[TensorRT-LLM](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/tests/unittest/_torch/modeling)** — `test__sanity` + `test__allclose_to_hf` pattern, 29 model test files

candidates.title: Triton attention + CUDA graphs crashes on GB10/sm_121a — illegal memory access on first warmup inference
candidates.body:
**GPU:** NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121a, CUDA cap 12.1)
**Image:** lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20260303-145ae518
**Model:** Qwen3.5-122B-A10B NVFP4

**Symptoms:** Weights load fine, CUDA graph capture succeeds (~21s), server reports ready, first warmup POST crashes:
- Default (flashinfer sampling): `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered`
- With `--sampling-backend pytorch`: `asyncio.CancelledError` + 500 on first POST

**Workaround:** `--disable-cuda-graph` works correctly.

**Other notes:**
- `--attention-backend trtllm_mha` raises ValueError: check only matches SM100, not sm_121a (also Blackwell)
- Same setup on RTX 5090 (Ampere) works fine with CUDA graphs — sm_121a specific
- Crash is post-capture during warmup forward pass (triton kernel correctness on sm_121a?)

**Launch cmd:**
```
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /models/qwen3-5-122b-nvfp4 --quantization modelopt_fp4 --attention-backend triton --reasoning-parser qwen3 --context-length 16384
```

We found that it wasn't necessarily convenient or straightforward to get Kimi linear high perf serving in sgl. So we put together some bugs and perf tracking for convenience.

- [ ] cutlass_mla support (though it is ~ worse than trtllm_mla) https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/15788
- [ ] possible modelopt nvfp4/fp8 checkpoint
- [ ] Generate `E=256,N=256` triton config for triton 3.5.1 h200 / h100 (b200 use trtllm_mla)
- [x] Support piecewise cuda graph (this support piecewise with trtllm_mla) https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/15788
- [ ] https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/16186 ~5% e2e throughput improvement

# Bugs

-  fix trtllm_mla and flashinfer crash (trtllm_mla up to 18% improvement over triton). https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/15788

candidates.title: [Tracking] `DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp` Day 0 Support
candidates.body:
# Announcement

DeepSeek `DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp` model **Day 0 support on SGLang** is here! 🎉 Thanks to the joint efforts of the SGLang community, we now support this new model on H200, MI350 GPUs, and NPUs.

`DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp` builds upon `DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus` by incorporating [DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.11089) through continued training. With DSA—a fine-grained sparse attention mechanism powered by a lightning-fast indexer (already supported in SGLang)—DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp delivers significant efficiency improvements in both training and inference, especially for long-context scenarios.


## Installation

### Docker

```bash
# H200/B200
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:latest


# MI350/MI355
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dsv32-rocm

# NPUs
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dsv32-a2
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dsv32-a3
```

### Build from source

```bash
```bash
# Install SGLang
git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang
cd sglang
pip3 install pip --upgrade
pip3 install -e "python[all]"

# Install flash_mla
git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA.git flash-mla
cd flash-mla
git submodule update --init --recursive
pip install -v .
```

## Launch Command

```bash
# Launch with TP + DP
python -m sglang.launch_server --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp --tp 8 --dp 8 --enable-dp-attention

# Launch with EP + DP
python -m sglang.launch_server --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp --tp 8 --ep 8 --dp 8 --enable-dp-attention

# Launch with MTP
python -m sglang.launch_server --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp --tp 8 --dp 8 --enable-dp-attention --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4
```

## Future Plan

- [x] PR to merge: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/11061
- [x] Support B200.
- [x] Support FP8 KV cache.
- [x] MTP: #11652
- [x] PD Disaggregation: #10912
- [ ] Tilelang kernels for flexible deployment.
- [x] Support GB200. 
- [x] Enable pure TP #13646
- [ ] Optimization tracked in #11989

candidates.title: [RFC] Recursive Tensor Collector: Fix CUDA Graph Invalidation After Weight Reload
candidates.body:
**Related Issue:** [vllm#48312](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48312) (Category 1: Storage Identity)
**Related PRs:** [#48251](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48251), [#48438](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48438), [#48539](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48539), [#41670](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41670)

## Summary

We propose a **generic, infrastructure-level** fix for CUDA graph invalidation caused by unmanaged tensor address drift during `reload_weights()`. The solution recursively discovers all CUDA tensors reachable from each `nn.Module` layer -- including those on nested Python objects like kernel instances, quant methods, and `functools.partial` -- and extends the existing copy-back mechanism to preserve their device addresses across reloads.

This eliminates an entire class of bugs (13 confirmed/high-risk sites) without requiring changes to any individual kernel, quantization scheme, or attention implementation.

## Background: Lifecycle of Model Loading, CUDA Graph Capture, and Weight Reload

### End-to-end timeline

The following diagram shows the chronological order of all key events. Understanding this order is essential to understanding the bug:

```
Time ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

[1] Initial Load              [2] CUDA Graph Capture        [3] Normal Inference
load_model()                  (lazy, on first inference)    (graph replay)
├─ load_weights()             ├─ CUDAGraphWrapper           ├─ .replay()
├─ process_weights_after_     │  .__call__()                ├─ .replay()
│  loading()                  │  torch.cuda.graph():        ├─ .replay()
│  creates workspace @addr_A  │   records forward pass      │  ...
│  creates W_UV    @addr_B    │   burns in addr_A, B, C     │
│  creates strides @addr_C    │   into the graph            │
│                             │                             │

                                                    RL framework updates weights
                                                            │
                                                            ▼

[4] reload_weights()                                [5] Resume Inference
├─ initialize_layerwise_reload()  ← inside reload   ├─ .replay()
│  ├─ snapshot old tensors (addr_A, B, C)            │  still uses addr_A, B, C
│  ├─ collect extra_tensor_slots                     │  but now with new values
│  ├─ move params to meta device                     │
│  └─ wrap weight_loaders                            │
├─ model.load_weights(new_weights)                   │
│  └─ per-layer _layerwise_process():                │
│     ├─ materialize (allocate new GPU memory)        │
│     ├─ load new weights                             │
│     ├─ process_weights_after_loading()              │
│     │  creates NEW workspace @addr_D                │
│     │  creates NEW W_UV     @addr_E                 │
│     ├─ copy-back:                                   │
│     │  addr_A.copy_(new workspace val)  ← existing  │
│     │  addr_B.copy_(new W_UV val)       ← OUR FIX   │
│     │  re-attach old tensors to layer                │
│     │  (addr_D, addr_E tensors discarded)           │
├─ finalize_layerwise_reload()                        │
└─ reset_encoder_cache()                              │
```

**Key chronological order:**

```
[1] load_model  →  [2] CUDA Graph Capture  →  [3] Inference  →  [4] reload_weights  →  [5] Inference
```

- **[1] happens once** at engine startup. `process_weights_after_loading()` creates derived tensors (workspace, W_UV, strides, etc.) at addresses A, B, C.
- **[2] happens lazily** on the first inference request for each batch size. `torch.cuda.graph()` records the forward pass and **burns in addresses A, B, C** -- the graph will always read/write these exact addresses on replay.
- **[3] is the steady state.** Each inference call just does `entry.cudagraph.replay()` -- no Python, no tensor lookups, just replaying recorded GPU operations at recorded addresses.
- **[4] is triggered by the RL framework** after training updates weights. `initialize_layerwise_reload()` is called **inside** `reload_weights()`, not as a separate step. After reload, `process_weights_after_loading()` creates new tensors at addresses D, E -- but the copy-back mechanism writes new values into old addresses A, B, C and discards D, E.
- **[5] resumes inference.** Graph replay reads addresses A, B, C. If copy-back worked correctly, these contain the new values. If any address was missed, the graph reads stale/freed/garbage memory.

### Where CUDA graphs are captured

CUDA graphs are captured lazily by `CUDAGraphWrapper.__call__()` (`compilation/cuda_graph.py:233-361`). The first time a given batch size is seen during inference, the wrapper records the entire forward pass:

```python
# compilation/cuda_graph.py:265-337 (simplified)
class CUDAGraphWrapper:
    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        entry = self.concrete_cudagraph_entries[batch_descriptor]

        if entry.cudagraph is None:
            # First time for this batch size -> capture
            cudagraph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
            with torch.cuda.graph(cudagraph, pool=self.graph_pool, stream=...):
                output = self.runnable(*args, **kwargs)  # record all CUDA ops
            entry.cudagraph = cudagraph
            return output

        # Subsequent calls -> replay the recorded ops directly on GPU
        entry.cudagraph.replay()
        return entry.output
```

During capture, `torch.cuda.graph()` records every CUDA kernel launch and **burns in the `data_ptr()` of every tensor** accessed by those kernels. On replay, the GPU executes the recorded kernel sequence directly -- no Python code runs, no tensor lookups happen. The GPU just reads/writes the exact memory addresses that were recorded.

**Critical design decision: `reload_weights()` does NOT clear or re-capture CUDA graphs.** The `reload_weights()` code path (`gpu_model_runner.py:5514-5518`) has no call to `CUDAGraphWrapper.clear_all_graphs()` or any re-capture logic. This is intentional -- re-capturing graphs is expensive and would negate the performance benefit of hot-reload in RL loops.

This means **the entire burden of correctness falls on the copy-back mechanism**: after reload, every tensor address that a CUDA graph references must still be valid and contain the correct (updated) values. If any address drifts, the consequences depend on what happened to the old memory:

| Scenario | Symptom |
|----------|---------|
| Old address reused by PyTorch allocator for another tensor | Silent wrong output (reads unrelated data) |
| Old address still allocated but holds stale values | Silent wrong output (reads old weights) |
| Old address freed back to OS / CUDA driver | `illegal memory access` (process crash) |
| Old address was Marlin workspace (atomic counter) | Garbage counter value -> kernel infinite wait -> **livelock** (confirmed: 100% GPU for >10 min on RTX 4090) |

### What does layerwise reload do? (step [4] in detail)

`reload_weights()` (`gpu_model_runner.py:5468`) calls three functions in sequence:

```python
initialize_layerwise_reload(model)          # prepare
loaded_weights = model.load_weights(iter)   # load
finalize_layerwise_reload(model, config)    # finalize
```

The name "layerwise" means it processes **one layer at a time** to minimize peak GPU memory (avoids having both old and new weights for the entire model simultaneously).

**`initialize_layerwise_reload()`** (`layerwise.py:84-126`) -- For each `nn.Module` layer:
1. **Snapshot kernel tensors** (`line 112`): Save references to current `_parameters` and `_buffers` -- these hold the addresses that CUDA graphs burned in.
2. **Collect extra tensor slots** (`line 119`): Recursively find unmanaged CUDA tensors on the layer (**our addition**).
3. **Restore to meta device** (`line 122`): Move all params/buffers to meta device (zero GPU memory), freeing space for new weights.
4. **Wrap weight loaders** (`line 125`): Replace each param's `weight_loader` with a wrapper that buffers incoming weights.

**`model.load_weights()`** -- Weights stream in one tensor at a time. The wrapper buffers them. When all weights for a layer are ready (`load_numel >= load_numel_total`), it triggers `_layerwise_process()` (`layerwise.py:361-401`):
1. **Materialize** (`line 372`): Allocate real GPU memory for this layer
2. **Load** (`line 384-387`): Copy buffered weights into the new GPU tensors
3. **Post-process** (`line 390-392`): Run `process_weights_after_loading()` -- **this creates new derived tensors at new addresses**
4. **Copy-back** (`line 396-398`): Copy new values into old addresses, restore references

**`finalize_layerwise_reload()`** (`layerwise.py:234-306`) -- Handles Attention/MLA layers (deferred until all linear layers are done) and layers with padding.

### The copy-back mechanism and its gap

The critical function is `_copy_and_restore_kernel_tensors()` (`layerwise.py:417-433`):

```python
def _copy_and_restore_kernel_tensors(layer, info):
    parameters, buffers = info.kernel_tensors  # saved in Phase 1

    for name, param in parameters.items():
        param.data.copy_(getattr(layer, name))  # new values -> old address
    for name, buffer in buffers.items():
        buffer.data.copy_(getattr(layer, name))  # new values -> old address

    _place_kernel_tensors(layer, info)  # re-attach old tensors to layer
```

This ensures that after reload, `layer.qweight.data_ptr()` is the same address CUDA graph captured -- but with updated values. **The problem is that it only covers `layer._parameters` and `layer._buffers`.**

## Motivation

### The Problem

`process_weights_after_loading()` creates *derived tensors* -- workspaces, stride descriptors, fused scales, permutation indices -- stored as **plain Python attributes** on `nn.Module`, kernel objects, or quant method instances. These are invisible to `_parameters`/`_buffers` and therefore invisible to the copy-back mechanism:

```
layer (nn.Module)
|-- _parameters: {qweight, scales, g_idx}        <- copy-back covers these
|-- _buffers: {}                                   <- copy-back covers these
|-- g_idx_sort_indices (bare Tensor)               <- MISSED
|-- W_UV, W_UK_T (bare Tensor)                     <- MISSED
`-- quant_method (Python object)
    `-- kernel (Python object)
        `-- workspace (Tensor)                     <- MISSED
    `-- moe_kernel (Python object)
        `-- fused_experts (Python object)
            |-- ab_strides1 (Tensor)               <- MISSED
            |-- ab_strides2 (Tensor)               <- MISSED
            `-- c_strides1 (Tensor)                <- MISSED
```

After reload, these tensors get new addresses. CUDA graph replay reads the old (now stale or freed) addresses, causing:
- **Illegal memory access** (segfault/CUDA error)
- **Silent wrong outputs** (reading stale data at old addresses)
- **Graph replay livelock** (Marlin workspace used as thread-block synchronization counter; garbage value causes infinite wait -- confirmed on RTX 4090: 100% GPU utilization for >10 minutes)

### Scale of the Problem

We identified **13 affected sites** across the codebase through static audit + live verification:

| # | Component | Affected Tensors | Severity |
|---|-----------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | Generic MLA ([#48251](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48251)) | `W_UV`, `W_UK_T` | Wrong output |
| 2 | AITER MoE shuffle ([#40390](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40390)) | `w13_weight`, `w2_weight` | Wrong output (fixed) |
| 3 | ROCm MoE padding ([#46009](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46009)) | `.data` storage swap | Wrong output |
| 4 | CUTLASS FP8 MoE ([#41670](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41670)) | `ab_strides*`, `c_strides*` | Illegal memory access |
| 5 | Marlin workspace + sort indices ([#48438](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48438)) | `workspace`, `g_idx_sort_indices` | Livelock / wrong output |
| 6 | 8 Marlin siblings (FP8/FP4/MoE variants) | `workspace` in each | Livelock |
| 7 | AITER MLA FP4/FP8 | `W_K`, `W_V`, `*_scale` | Wrong output (audit) |
| 8 | FlashInfer B12x MoE | `_fc2_input_scale`, `w*_sf_mma` | Wrong output (audit) |
| 9 | Compressed-tensors NVFP4 CUTLASS MoE | `g1/g2_alphas`, `a*/gscale` | Wrong output (audit) |
| 10 | CUTLASS W4A8 FP8 MoE | `a_strides*`, `c_strides*`, `s_strides*` | Illegal memory access (audit) |
| 11 | RDNA3 WNA16 MoE | `rdna3_w1_buf`, `rdna3_act_buf` | Wrong output (audit) |
| 12 | Machete act-order | `act_perm` | Wrong output (audit) |
| 13 | Compressed-tensors WNA8O8 | cloned scales | Wrong output (audit) |

**All 13 sites share the same root cause:** tensors created by `process_weights_after_loading()` that live outside `_parameters`/`_buffers`. Fixing them one by one is a game of whack-a-mole; any new kernel or quant method can introduce the same bug. We need a systematic solution.

## Proposed Solution

### Design

Extend the layerwise reload pipeline with a **recursive tensor collector** that discovers all CUDA tensors reachable from each layer's attribute tree, and a **copy-back extension** that restores their addresses after reload.

```
                     Current Pipeline              Enhanced Pipeline
                  +------------------+          +------------------+
Snapshot          | _parameters      |          | _parameters      |
(before reload)   | _buffers         |          | _buffers         |
                  |                  |          | + bare attrs     |
                  |                  |          | + nested objects  |
                  +------------------+          +------------------+
                         |                            |
PWAL creates new tensors (same)                      (same)
                         |                            |
Copy-back         | params & buffers |          | params & buffers |
(after reload)    | only             |          | + ALL tracked    |
                  |                  |          |   tensors        |
                  +------------------+          +------------------+
```

### Key Components

#### 1. `tensor_collector.py` -- Recursive Discovery

```python
def collect_extra_tensors(layer: nn.Module) -> list[TensorSlot]:
    """
    Recursively walk layer's attribute tree, collecting all CUDA tensors
    NOT already in _parameters/_buffers.

    Traversal covers:
    - Plain tensor attributes on the module (Type A)
    - Tensors on nested Python objects: kernel, quant_method, experts (Type B)
    - Tensors inside dicts, lists, tuples
    - Tensors captured in functools.partial args/kwargs
    - Tensors captured in function closures

    Does NOT recurse into child nn.Modules (they have their own reload cycle).
    Deduplicates by storage id (handles shared-storage aliases).
    Max depth = 8 (safety bound; real paths are ~4-5 levels deep).
    """
```

Each discovered tensor is recorded as a `TensorSlot`:

```python
@dataclass
class TensorSlot:
    path: str              # e.g. "quant_method.kernel.workspace"
    tensor: torch.Tensor   # strong ref (prevents GC of old address)
    data_ptr: int          # address at capture time
    storage_id: int        # for deduplication
```

#### 2. `path_resolver.py` -- Object Graph Navigation

```python
def resolve_path(root, path: str) -> torch.Tensor | None:
    """Navigate 'quant_method.kernel.workspace' from root object."""

def set_by_path(root, path: str, value: torch.Tensor) -> bool:
    """Set attribute at path to value, returning success."""
```

Handles dotted paths, dict/list indexing (`some_dict['key']`, `some_list[0]`).

#### 3. Integration into `layerwise.py`

Three surgical modifications:

```python
# 1. Snapshot phase: collect extra tensors alongside params/buffers
def initialize_layerwise_reload(model):
    for layer in model.modules():
        info = get_layerwise_info(layer)
        info.kernel_tensors = get_layer_params_buffers(layer)
        info.extra_tensor_slots = collect_extra_tensors(layer)  # NEW
        ...

# 2. Restore phase: copy-back extra tensors after PWAL
def _copy_and_restore_kernel_tensors(layer, info):
    # ... existing param/buffer copy-back ...
    _copy_back_extra_tensors(layer, info)  # NEW

# 3. New function: extra tensor copy-back
def _copy_back_extra_tensors(layer, info):
    for slot in info.extra_tensor_slots:
        new_tensor = resolve_path(layer, slot.path)
        if compatible(slot.tensor, new_tensor):  # shape + dtype check
            slot.tensor.data.copy_(new_tensor)           # new values -> old address
            set_by_path(layer, slot.path, slot.tensor)   # old tensor -> object graph
```

### Why This Works Even When Entire Objects Are Replaced

Consider CUTLASS FP8 MoE where `process_weights_after_loading()` creates an entirely new `CutlassExpertsFp8` instance:

```python
self.moe_kernel = make_fp8_moe_kernel(...)  # brand new object
```

The copy-back still works because:
1. `slot.tensor` holds a **strong reference** to the old tensor -- it won't be GC'd
2. `resolve_path()` navigates to the **new object's** attribute (new stride tensor)
3. `old_tensor.data.copy_(new_tensor)` writes new values into the **old address**
4. `set_by_path()` sets the **new object's** attribute to point to the **old tensor**

Result: the new `CutlassExpertsFp8` object's `ab_strides1` now points to the old address with new values. CUDA graph replay reads correct data from the unchanged address.

### Properties

- **Zero changes to kernel/quant/attention code**: Pure infrastructure fix in `reload/`
- **Forward-compatible**: New kernels that create derived tensors are automatically covered
- **Safe defaults**: Shape/dtype mismatches are logged and skipped (no crash), with a signal for graph recapture
- **Minimal memory overhead**: Extra tensor slots hold strong refs to small tensors (workspaces, strides, indices); negligible vs model weights
- **Storage deduplication**: Shared-storage aliases (e.g., `c_strides2 = ab_strides1`) are handled correctly

**No changes to:**
